nameStory: Rattlesnake master earned its intriguing name from Native American and early settler beliefs that the plant could cure snakebites or repel rattlesnakes. The name 'button eryngo' comes from its distinctive round, spiky flower heads that look like thorny buttons stuck on top of sturdy stems.
description: Rattlesnake master is a striking perennial herb that looks more like a yucca plant than a typical member of the carrot family. It forms clumps of long, narrow, sword-like leaves that can grow 2-4 feet tall, topped with unusual round, spiky flower heads on thick stems. The plant has a very architectural, almost sculptural appearance that makes it stand out dramatically from other prairie and meadow plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive round, button-like flower heads about 1 inch across, densely packed with tiny white to greenish-white flowers surrounded by spiny bracts that feel sharp to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, sword-shaped leaves that are parallel-veined and feel tough and leathery, growing in a basal rosette and looking remarkably like yucca leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinctive clumps with leaves radiating from the base, sending up sturdy, branched flowering stems that rise well above the foliage

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy flowering stems that feel rigid and substantial, often with a bluish or whitish cast, branching near the top to hold multiple flower heads

habitat: In New England, rattlesnake master is extremely rare and found only in a few scattered locations in Connecticut and possibly nearby states. It prefers sunny, well-drained prairie-like habitats, sandy soils, and open meadows where it won't be shaded out by taller vegetation.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the base, forming the characteristic sword-like rosette that grows throughout the season.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer with its distinctive spiky button flowers that attract various small insects and beetles.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads turn brown and develop into spiky seed heads that persist, while leaves may begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and seed heads often persist through winter, and the tough basal leaves may remain somewhat evergreen in milder conditions.

funFact: Despite being in the carrot family (Apiaceae), rattlesnake master's flowers look nothing like typical umbrella-shaped carrot family blooms - instead, its spiky round flower heads are so unusual that many people mistake it for a completely different plant family entirely!
confusionNotes: The sword-like leaves are most commonly confused with yucca plants, but yucca leaves are typically thicker and more succulent-feeling, and yuccas produce tall spikes of large white bell-shaped flowers rather than small round spiky balls.
contextualKnowledge: This plant represents one of New England's rarest prairie remnants - it's much more common in the Midwest's tallgrass prairies, so finding it in New England is like discovering a piece of the Great Plains that somehow got stranded in the East.
compareHints: Unlike its European relatives Blue Eryngo and Italian Eryngo (which are sometimes grown in gardens), rattlesnake master has much longer, more yucca-like leaves and tends to be a larger, more robust plant overall. The other eryngos typically have more divided, thistle-like leaves and smaller stature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue eryngo differs from its cousin rattlesnake master by having much smaller, more numerous blue flower heads rather than rattlesnake master's larger, white, golf ball-sized flower clusters.
Italian Eryngo differs from its cousin Rattlesnake Master by having deeply lobed, spiny basal leaves instead of long, narrow sword-like leaves, and much more colorful blue-purple stems and bracts.
